Adult Naked-belly searobin (Bellator gymnostethus) reach a maximum total length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], a size achieved by females in particular. This asymptotic length is rather modest compared to some congeneric species, suggesting a life history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction over continued somatic expansion. Field surveys along the Atlantic coast indicate that individuals attain this maximum size within a few years, after which growth slows considerably. The relationship between length and mass follows a typical cubic function for triglid fishes, with the largest females weighing approximately 49.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 49.9 grams] at full maturity. This adult body mass is consistent with values reported for other benthic-dwelling scorpaeniforms of similar dimensions. The species' demersal habits and diet of small crustaceans likely contribute to its relatively small size compared to more pelagic members of the family.

Sexual maturation in Bellator gymnostethus occurs at a total length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 5 grams [Wwp = 5 grams]. This reproductive size is approximately half the ultimate length, a pattern commonly observed in fishes with determinate or asymptotic growth. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from trawl-collected specimens confirms that individuals at this length exhibit active gametogenesis, marking the onset of reproductive capability. The relatively small size at puberty suggests that this species can begin contributing to the next generation within its first year of life under favorable conditions. This early maturation likely represents an adaptation to the high levels of natural mortality typical of small-bodied demersal fishes on the continental shelf.

Reproductive output in Naked-belly searobin is best understood by examining both fecundity per event and spawning frequency. Data derived from related species such as Prionotus evolans, adjusted for body size, indicate that females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] at a water temperature of 20.1 °C [T = 20.1 °C]. Each reproductive event yields approximately 82 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 82 eggs per clutch], a value scaled from the known maximum daily rate for a 15-centimeter individual. This annual reproductive strategy contrasts with the multiple-batch spawning observed in some tropical triglids, suggesting that temperature and seasonality constrain the duration of the spawning window for this species. The relatively modest clutch size is offset by the extended spawning season, allowing for sustained recruitment over several months.

Eggs of Bellator gymnostethus are demersal and adhesive, with a mean wet weight at birth of 0.0008 grams [Wwb = 0.0008 grams]. This value is derived from an egg diameter range of 1.05 to 1.25 millimeters, a size typical of triglid fishes. The incubation period proceeds for 10 days [ab = 10 days] before eclosion occurs at a water temperature of 20.1 °C [T = 20.1 °C]. This relatively rapid development is characteristic of warm-water demersal spawners, where elevated temperatures accelerate embryogenesis. The small egg size and short incubation period suggest a high potential for larval dispersal, as the yolk-sac larvae enter the plankton soon after hatching. The chorion is transparent, allowing for observation of the developing embryo through the egg capsule. Furthermore, the pelagic larval phase following yolk-sac absorption lasts several weeks, during which the larvae feed on copepod nauplii and other small zooplankton, a period of high vulnerability to predation that shapes early survival rates. This extended planktonic interval contrasts with the direct development observed in some confamilial species and likely facilitates broad geographic dispersal via coastal currents, linking local populations across considerable distances along the continental shelf.

The maximum lifespan of Bellator gymnostethus is approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] when measured at a stable water temperature of 20.1 °C [T = 20.1 °C]. This longevity is relatively extended for a fish of its size, suggesting that the species experiences low natural mortality once it reaches adulthood. The combination of early maturation and an extended reproductive lifespan allows for multiple spawning seasons over the course of an individual's life. The age at first reproduction aligns closely with the attainment of sexual maturity, as the species does not exhibit a prolonged period of adolescent sterility. This life history syndrome, characterized by modest size, early maturity, and moderate longevity, is typical of demersal fishes inhabiting stable continental shelf environments.
